0: In the past, making a product marketing poster usually involved several stages: preparing assets, designing the background, laying out the product, adding copy and adjusting the size. If the same product also had to go to several platforms, designers often had to rework the layout for each size.
1: Today, text-to-image, image-to-image, local editing and model fine-tuning can be chained together into a fairly complete marketing content pipeline covering idea generation, product design, image revision and size adaptation.
2: For example, a drinks product needs a “summer marketing” poster with ice cubes, splashes, lemon and green leaves. You can first generate an initial marketing image quickly from a text description, then combine it with the product photo for image-to-image editing, add the brand logo, and keep revising individual elements as needed. Finally you can extend the same marketing image into different sizes for social media, short video and web ads.
3: This chapter takes the FRESH DAY summer drink marketing image as an example and shows how to build a simple AIGC marketing content pipeline on the open image-generation models in ModelScope. The experiment starts from text-to-image and moves through image-to-image, keeping the product subject, local editing, size adaptation and a brand-style LoRA.
5: Text-to-image means generating an image directly from a text description. You do not need a complete set of design assets: describe the scene you want through a prompt — theme, subject, background, colour, composition, visual style — and the model generates the corresponding image.
6: For marketing content, text-to-image suits idea exploration and generating an initial visual concept. Before making a summer drink poster, you can tell the model you want “a fresh summer mood, ice cubes, splashes, lemon, blue-green tones, commercial photography style” and let it generate a complete marketing image quickly. Compared with designing from a blank canvas, this shows you different ideas faster.
7: The open community already offers many image-generation models, such as Stable Diffusion, FLUX, Qwen-Image and Z-Image-Turbo. They differ in image quality, prompt understanding, text rendering and hardware needs
8: This section uses the Z-Image-Turbo model on ModelScope for the text-to-image experiment. The Turbo version is optimised for generation efficiency and can produce an image in fewer inference steps, which suits individual developers and experiment environments with limited GPU resources.

18: Text-to-image is great for generating marketing ideas and background concepts quickly, but it has an obvious problem: if you ask the model to generate a specific product directly, the packaging, logo and text may differ from the real product. In a formal product marketing scenario you still need to work from a real product photo.
19: Text-to-image relies mainly on a text description, whereas image-to-image takes both a reference image and a text description. The model can refer to the product subject, packaging and composition in the original image, then adjust the background, lighting and marketing elements according to the prompt.
20: This section uses SenseNova-U1.5-8B-MoT as the image-editing model. It supports text-to-image and image editing and can understand both the input image and the text instruction, adjusting the specified content in the original image according to the prompt. Compared with generating from text alone, SenseNova-U1.5-8B-MoT can use the visual information in the input image and, while keeping the subject and overall structure, modify the packaging, background, colours and decorative elements — which makes it well suited to generating and editing product marketing images.
21: The experiment continues from the summer drink image generated in the previous section, editing it with the image-to-image model. While keeping the bottle as the subject and the overall structure, we add the “FRESH DAY” brand logo to the bottle and bring in summer elements such as ice cubes, splashes and lemon, producing a more complete product marketing image. The default SenseNova-U1.5-8B-MoT loading mode runs out of VRAM, so this code uses a low-VRAM loading mode to reduce the footprint.
25: Compared with generating entirely from text, image-to-image can use the visual information in the original image and is better suited to cases where you already have product assets or a reference design. From the image above you can also see that it still differs from what was actually wanted: even with a real product photo supplied, the model may redraw parts of the product. In real use you also need to consider keeping the product subject and local editing.
27: In real applications of product marketing images, besides looking good you need the product information to be accurate. The bottle's appearance, packaging structure and brand logo are usually core visual information about the product; if they change noticeably during editing, the generated image may no longer match the actual product. When editing with an image-generation model, be clear about what must be kept and what may change. For example, you can ask the model to keep the bottle, the brand logo and the overall composition unchanged and adjust only the background, decorative elements or local objects. Stating these constraints in the prompt reduces how much the model regenerates the product subject and makes the result more controllable.

This example shows how prompts can make image editing more controllable.

32: Once a product marketing image is finished it usually has to be published to different platforms. Because each platform displays content differently, the requirements on image size and aspect ratio vary. Social media often uses 1:1 or 4:5, short-video platforms prefer 9:16 vertical, and web banners and landscape ads usually use 16:9. Resizing the original directly can stretch or squash the product, so while keeping the product subject unchanged we can use an image-editing model to outpaint the image, adding background and decorative content around the edges for the target ratio.
33: Outpainting differs from ordinary resizing. It does not simply change the length and width of the original; it generates new areas based on the content and style of the existing image. For example, converting a vertical drink marketing image to 16:9 landscape can keep the bottle's size and proportion largely unchanged while extending the background, splashes, ice cubes and green leaves to the sides, so the new areas blend naturally with the original.

37: With text-to-image and image-to-image models you can generate different kinds of marketing images quickly, but because each generation has some randomness, even with the same or a similar prompt, images from different batches can differ in colour, composition, lighting and overall visual style.
38: For corporate marketing you usually want different promotional assets to keep a fairly consistent brand visual style. This section introduces LoRA fine-tuning: prepare a set of marketing images with a consistent visual style, train the model on them so it learns that particular colour, composition and look, and it will then present the required brand visual features more reliably in later generations.
39: This experiment fine-tunes Z-Image-Turbo with LoRA. The main reason is that the model meets the needs of the earlier text-to-image experiment and, compared with the SenseNova-U1.5-8B-MoT used in the image-to-image part, needs fewer VRAM resources for training, which makes it better suited to completing a LoRA fine-tuning experiment on a single card with 24 GB of VRAM. If you have more GPU VRAM and compute, you can also try fine-tuning SenseNova-U1.5-8B-MoT with LoRA.
